An intense and extensive inflammation had seized
upon the bowels, and, in my opinion, upon the

countered, which, setting at naught the highest
science and the best directed efforts of human
skill, runs almost from the very outset steadily
and rapidly into fatal termination. I had seen
similar cases before; and am particularly remind
ed by it of that of the late Senator Fulton, who
was, alike in station, in disease, and in death, the
predecessor of him whose loss we now deplore.


Col. A. ASHLEY was a native of New England—


the 1st day of June 1800; and, consequently, at
the time of his death, was in the 48th year of
his age. When an infant only three months, he

town of Hudson, in New York. He grew up,
engaged in the practice of the law, and resided
there about 31 years; then migrated to Illinois,
where he remained about two years, and subse-

afterwards he married in Missouri, and removed,
with his young family, to his home in the wilder-

the far west was no trivial undertaking. It
required high degree of enterprise to encounter
the privations, hardships, and perils of frontier
life—now so much talked about, but then actually
endured. An uncommon share of mental fore-
cast would alone suffice to ascertain a point in
so wide range, which must become the centre
of important operations, from which settlement
and civilization must radiate, and then throw
back an accumulated interest. A firmness, fixed-
ness, singleness of purpose, true to its object as
the needle to the pole, was alone capable of abid-

provement, then no bigger than a man's hand,
which was, within quarter of a century, to cov-

true wants of human society—monuments made
up the wilderness reclaimed and converted into
cultivated fields; of the towns, with their bristling

teeming commerce of finical seas; and

securely under their own roof-trees, and stand in

own broad acres. In short, the noble aggre-
gate of these monuments is before the world, in
the peerless prosperity of "the great West."

montane stripling, as the type of a class. And of

MIXING SOILS.—There is often an advantage in mixing soils which will pay well for the labor. It is almost always the case that when digging wells or cellars, some of the bottom of the earth, which comes from a depth of several feet from the surface of the ground, be spread upon land that has been sometime cultivated, or even upon grasslands, a stimulus is given to the crop that is quite surprising.

A year or two ago, we visited a farmer in one of the upper counties in this State, whom we found caring coarse, gravelly loam into his barnyard. He stated that he found much benefit with such material among his barn-yard manure, and fancied that the juices of the manure dissolves a part of the gravel or something else, and that produced the benefit to his crops. We supposed, however, that it was owing to the mixing of soils, by which, not only the texture of the surface soils was changed, but probably other materials, or ingredients supplied that were lacking in the soil which received the dressing. We all know that after draining a boggy piece of ground, if there be any chance to mix sand, gravel or loam with it, manifest improvement is effected; and we also know that if the muck of a peak of the bog is hauled on the upland, and its acids neutralized by long exposure to the weather, or to ashes, &c., great benefit is obtained; so also if sand or gravel be hauled upon stiff clays, or clay put on sandy and gravelly soils, mutual improvement is effected. Perhaps the benefit would not always pay for the expenses, but where the mixing can be done easily and at reasonable cost, it is oftentimes a good plan to mix them thoroughly.—Maine Farmer.

Mr. EDITOR:—I am mortified but not disappointed at the result of the recent vote in Vermont on the question of license; it is as expected. The reason is perfectly plain. The Presidential election comes next fall and neither of the rival parties dares to offend the rum interest for fear of losing votes. So they allow rum to triumph for the time being. Perhaps next year, when the Presidential question is decided, they will not be afraid to talk more and act more.


Now we can see from such examples as this the great benefits resulting to society from party spirit. It is perfectly plain to any disinterested man that neither of these parties cares for any thing but power and its emoluments. Of course, in the selection of candidates for office, in performing the duties incident to power, little if any thing else is taken into consideration but the prospective interests of party. This is paramount to every thing else. Temperance, liberty and religion may be made much of when they do not come in collision with or endanger these interests. But when an election is at hand they are discarded; I have seen this verified too often to doubt its truth.


Now do not expect to see much progress made in any good cause which can be relied on as real or efficient, while its advocates are spell-bound and tied neck and heels to these pro-slavery parties. Such progress could it be accomplished would be one of the greatest anomalies or monstrosities in nature. There is too much corruption in these parties to admit of the least hope or possibility of such an emanation from them. Their objects are too base and sordid and their measures correspond with their objects. Take away the interests of slavery from them and they would be like beasts without head, or ships without a rudder. They would be bewildered and amazed at their position, and would not know how to act. It would be a long time before their trembling knees would recover sufficient strength to stand erect like men. I am not sure but this state of things is anticipated, and that this may be one reason for the great aversion to change.


Now, how long shall we wait for a better state of things? And how can it be brought about? Is there not honesty and intelligence enough among the people to discard slavery, and other children of the Devil? If there is, why is it not brought into action to some purpose?


I believe these evils will continue and increase until they are sensibly checked, and until that same spirit of selfishness which sustains them, will find to its cost that the viper nourished with so much care, returns the favor by a bitter sting. Selfishness is mostly power which in most cases is of far more potency than any considerations of right, truth, justice or religion. The worst of it is that this spirit is not often aroused until too late. Thousands have refused to aid the temperance cause until some of their nearest and dearest friends fell into a drunkard's grave, and often until they fell themselves victims. Pain and suffering are two prominent agents made use of by the Deity in the government of mankind and to punish the disobedience of his laws. When we have suffered enough to arouse us, then we begin to look about for the causes, and devise remedies mean for their removal. When the people generally take pains to inform themselves in relation to the evils of society, they will begin to act, and take the work of reformation into their own hands. This is the only remedy. A man's professions are worse than nothing if his actions give them the lie. Something more than mere profession is wanted. We have profession enough to save the universe if there were actions to correspond. The professions of party are infinitely less valuable than those of individuals. The latter may be held responsible in a certain sense, but in party the responsibility is divided and subdivided into the Homeopathic principle, into such small parts that it cannot be found. Like the Irishman's fear—"if you lay your finger on it and it is not there." This at least is the actual state of things, not what it ought to be—I admit.


A new law has been proposed, and has received some attention in the Massachusetts Legislature in reference to the sale of spirits without license. It is more stringent than the old one, and will be more efficient if carried into effect in accordance with it. Spirit imprisonment is one grade of punishment provided for our gentle violators of the law and judges from past observation have no doubt it is a needed feature. The rum party are red hot against it, which shows that there is some reason in the law, as well as for it. Whether it will pass or not is uncertain.


Yours truly, A. H. B.

We continue our extracts from Mr. Willard's pamphlet, on the peculiarities of Western river life.

No land has received such benefit as the West from the invention of the steamboat. There, in especial, ought the name of the inventor to be handed down with glory to the generations to come. No triumph of art over the obstacles of nature has ever been so complete. But for this invention, this valley might not have sustained a nation of farmers and planters; and the comforts, the arts, refinement and intelligence of the day would have made their way slowly from New Orleans to the Lakes, of the Mississippi and the Rocky Mountains. Thousands of boatmen would have been slowly and laboriously warping, and rowing, and polling, and cordelling their boats in three months' trip up these mighty and long streams, which are now accented by steamboats, in ten days. It may be safely asserted, that in many respects, the improvements of fifty years without steamboats, were brought to this country in few years after their invention. The distant points of the Ohio and the Mississippi used to be separated by distances and obstacles of transit more formidable in the passing, than the Atlantic. These points are now brought into juxtaposition. Distances on the rivers are not indeed annihilated, but they are diminished to about an eighth of their former extent and their difficulties and dangers are reduced even more than that. All the advantages of long rivers, such variety of soil, climate, productions remain invested of all the disadvantages of distance and difficulty of ascent. The day that commemorates this invention, should be a holiday of interest, only second to that which gave birth to the nation.

It is perhaps necessary to have something of the experience, which we have had, of the slowness, difficulty and danger of propelling boats against the current of these long rivers, fully to estimate the advantages of this invention. We have assembled the Mississippi in this way for fifty days in succession. We have had but too much of the same kind of experience on the other streams. We consider ten miles a day good progress. It is now refreshing, and imparts feeling of energy and power to the beholder to see the large and beautiful steamboats, ascending up the eddies, as though on the wing. When they have run on the eddy and strike the current, it is still more a noble spectacle. The foam bursts in sheets quite over the deck. The boat quivers for a moment with the conclusion; and then, as though she had collected energy, and vanquished her enemy, she resumes her stately march, and mounts against the current ten or twelve miles an hour. We have travelled ten days together between New Orleans and Louisvile, more than an hundred miles a day against the stream. The difficulty of ascending used to be the only one that dreaded in the anticipation of a voyage of this kind. This difficulty has now disappeared, and the only one that remains is to furnish money for the trip. Even the expense, considering the luxury of the fare and accommodations, is more moderate than could be expected. A family in Pittsburg wishes to make a social visit to a kindred family on Red River. The trip as matters now stand, is but two thousand miles. Servants, baggage, or "pundar," as the phrase is, the family and the family dog, cat and parrot all proposed. Even the return is but a short voyage. Surely we must resist strong temptations if we do not become social people. You are invited to a breakfast at seventy miles distance. You go on board the passing steamboat and are transported during the night, to go in the morning and reach your appointment. The day will probably come, when the inhabitants of the warm and sickly regions of the lower points of the Mississippi will take their periodical migrations to the North with the geese and swans, and with them return to the South in the autumn.

We have compared the most beautiful steamboats of the Atlantic waters with those of the Mississippi and we have seen none, which, in splendor and striking effect upon the eye, and the luxury and comfort of accommodation, surpass the Western boats. We have been amused in observing an Atlantic stranger, who had heard described by the phrase, "a backwoods," taking his first survey of such a steamboat. If there be any ground of complaint, it is, that so much gorgeousness offends good taste, and seems to be in opposition to that social ease and comfort, which would be desired in such a place. Certainly there can be no comparison between the comfort of the passage from Cincinnati to New Orleans in such a steamboat and a voyage at sea. The barren and boundless expanse of waters soon tires upon every eve but a seaman; and then there are storms, and the necessity of fastening the tables, and of holding to something to keep in bed. There is the insupportable nausea of sea sickness and there is danger. Here we are always near the shore, always the green earth can always eat, write, and study, undisturbed. You can always obtain cream, fowls, vegetables, fruit, fresh meat and wild game in their season from the shore.

A stranger to this mode of travelling would find it difficult to describe his impressions upon descending the Mississippi for the first time in one of these steamboats, which we have named. He contemplates the prodigious construction, with its double tiers of cabins, and its separate establishment for the ladies, and its commodious arrangements for the deck passengers and the servants. Overhead about him, and below him, all is life and movement. He contemplates the splendor of the cabin, its beautiful finishing of the richest woods, its rich carpeting, its mirrors and fine furniture, its sliding tables, its ballroom, and all its arrangements for the accommodation of two hundred cabin passengers. The fare is sumptuous, and everything is in a style of splendor, order, and quiet far exceeding most city taverns. You read, converse, walk or sleep. You choose. You are not burdened by the restraint of useless ceremony. The varied and verdant scenery shifts about you. The trees, the green islands, the houses, the shore, everything has an appearance, as by enchantment, of moving past you. The river fowl, with their white and extended lines, are wheeling their flight above you. The sky is bright; the river is dotted with boats above, beside and below. The reception of Mr. Clay in New York is
said to have been most cordial, and on a mag-
nificent scale. In welcoming him to the city,


Mr. Franklin, who had been deputed for the pur-
pose, said—"We might as well undertake to still
the raging tempest and say to the winds, 'Be
still,' as to control the excitement of our people


when the Sage of Ashland treads upon their soil
and walks in their midst." The reply was most
eloquent; if Mr. Clay had any pre-
tensions to eloquence or to elocution, it cannot be
expected on this occasion, for two reasons. One
is that my heart is full, and the other is that the
subject is myself." In taking leave of the Philad-
elphia committee, Mr. Clay said:


"I have several times in my life had occasion
to be thankful for the friendship, the affectionate
attachment evinced toward me by my friends at
Philadelphia. But never have I had such proofs
of love and attachment shown to me as during
my last visit. It seemed to me as if the whole
city, all the houses, had discharged themselves of
their population to greet me during my short
stay among them."


Truly indeed has it been said, that no man
lives who has as many warm friends and who
would more willingly and anxiously submit to
any privations for his sake, than Mr. Clay.
